remaining: Explicit coding start/stop and complete conventional feature order.

proposedEvidenceNotCredited.supportingExcerpt: In a conventional messenger RNA, the 5-prime cap and untranslated region precede the protein-coding region, which runs from its initiation codon to a stop codon; the 3-prime untranslated region and adenosine tail follow it. Start-codon context describes bases around the start, including bases on both sides of the untranslated/coding boundary. It is not a separate segment inserted between those regions or a DNA transcription promoter. The cap belongs to the RNA rather than its delivery carrier, and the tail is RNA rather than part of the encoded protein.

proofs.requirement: Start context crosses the untranslated/coding boundary; it is not an extra inserted segment or a DNA transcription promoter. Untranslated regions can affect use of the message.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Start-codon context was tested by single-base substitutions around the AUG initiator in a cloned preproinsulin gene, where the best sequence identified changed proinsulin yield over a 20-fold range (Kozak). The interaction of the cap and the poly(A) tail was tested with luciferase mRNAs delivered by electroporation into tobacco protoplasts, Chinese hamster ovary cells and yeast, where the tail's effect depended on the cap (Gallie). A textbook describes the 5' cap, 5' and 3' untranslated regions that regulate translation initiation and mRNA stability, a poly-A tail of about 200 A residues added by poly-A polymerase to cellular mRNA, and a ribosome that moves from the cap to the AUG, with Kozak's rules describing the sequence around it (OpenStax Biology 2e). The cellular tail length is not a rule for engineered constructs: one dendritic-cell study found that a 120-nucleotide tail, an unmasked tail end and two 3' untranslated regions each improved stability and translation, and it measured transcript amount by RT-PCR, protein by eGFP, peptide-MHC density and T-cell stimulation separately (Holtkamp and colleagues), so a doubled reporter signal after a 3' change is one measurement, not a different antigen or a clinical benefit. These are tested constructs and cell systems, not one best sequence for a clinical product.

proofs.requirement: Codon composition and position-dependent RNA structure can affect RNA use and functional lifetime in defined cell/reporter systems; removing all structure is not a universal optimum.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In Mauger's engineered eGFP constructs, highly expressed messages could have highly structured coding regions, and coding-region structure affected the duration of active translation. This concerns the tested coding regions and does not show that removing every fold or maximising one codon score improves every message.

In four human cell lines, three independent methods showed that mRNA stability tracked codon identity rather than nucleotide content, stabilising codons tended to coincide with higher tRNA levels, and the effect depended on translation (Wu and colleagues, 2019). Another study separated codon usage from coding-region structure in eGFP constructs and defined functional half-life as the time an mRNA is actively translated, which differs from RNA that is merely present or protein that persists, so a doubled reporter signal at one time point does not show twice the RNA lifetime, a better neoantigen or any clinical effect (Mauger and colleagues).

evidence.supportingExcerpt: One documented origin is T7 polymerase initiating transcription from a promoter-less DNA end, producing an antisense strand and long double-stranded RNA that activated the sensor MDA5 (Mu and colleagues). In purification studies, unmodified mRNAs were translated better after HPLC purification but still induced high levels of cytokine secretion (Karikó and colleagues). A cellulose method removed at least 90 per cent of double-stranded RNA with over 65 per cent recovery regardless of mRNA length, coding sequence or nucleoside composition and increased translation in mice, and agarose gels showed that the purified mRNA stayed intact, but it removed duplexes of 30 base pairs or longer efficiently while most of a 21 base-pair duplex remained (Baiersdörfer and colleagues). Detection has its own scope: that paper notes an earlier report that about 40 base pairs of duplex are needed for detection by the J2 antibody, and a review of mRNA analytics lists immunoblot or ELISA for double-stranded RNA alongside separate integrity assays (Losada and colleagues). A lower dsRNA signal with worse fragmentation or recovery therefore does not show a better product. Method performance in those systems is not a clinical impurity limit.

A computational study of spacer design for class-I-restricted string-of-beads polypeptides reported a fivefold increase in predicted epitope recovery and a 44 per cent reduction in predicted neo-epitope immunogenicity compared with designs without spacers (Schubert and Kohlbacher); these are predictions, not measured protection. Combining an N-terminal leader peptide with an MHC class I trafficking signal at the C terminus improved presentation of class I and class II epitopes in human and mouse dendritic cells and expanded antigen-specific CD8 and CD4 T cells in vitro and in mice (Kreiter and colleagues). In a first-in-human RNA poly-neo-epitope melanoma study all patients developed T-cell responses against multiple vaccine neo-epitopes (Sahin and colleagues; abstract only), and each patient's vaccine in the Rojas pancreatic cancer trial used two uridine mRNA strands, each encoding up to 10 neoepitopes. Mass spectrometry can identify recovered HLA-bound peptides. Caron and colleagues' 2015 review describes class I peptides predominantly 9 to 12 amino acids long and reports that about 10 per cent of acquired spectra could be confidently assigned at a 1 per cent false discovery rate in the workflows discussed. It also describes evidence that mass spectrometry underestimates the self-HLA peptide repertoire, so non-detection does not prove absence. Prediction is not presentation: of more than 1,300 amino acid changes in two mouse tumour models about 13 per cent were predicted to bind MHC class I and a small fraction of those were confirmed by mass spectrometry (Yadav and colleagues). Because a single amino acid after an epitope changed its immunogenicity in a multiepitope DNA vaccine (Livingston and colleagues, already linked), a changed spacer is a changed construct that needs renewed processing and display evidence, while earlier evidence is retained for the parts that did not change.

proofs.requirement: Changing the spacer changes the combined protein and its boundaries: prior display of A does not establish the new construct, B display or either target's tumour recognition.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: An encoded antigen window is not necessarily the peptide eventually displayed. Joined windows and spacers can create new junction sequences. A protein-routing signal concerns the encoded protein rather than the particle delivery address. Identify any intended helper segment and test its HLA class II presentation and CD4 response in the relevant setting. Verify sequence and expression, recovered HLA-bound peptides and functional recognition separately; prediction scores do not supply a presentation threshold. Changing a spacer changes the construct even if two selected windows are unchanged. More encoded targets create opportunities only where relevant antigen expression, processing, compatible HLA presentation and functional recognition can occur. Target count alone is not measured response breadth.

A computational study of spacer design for class-I-restricted string-of-beads polypeptides reported a fivefold increase in predicted epitope recovery and a 44 per cent reduction in predicted neo-epitope immunogenicity compared with designs without spacers (Schubert and Kohlbacher); these are predictions, not measured protection. Combining an N-terminal leader peptide with an MHC class I trafficking signal at the C terminus improved presentation of class I and class II epitopes in human and mouse dendritic cells and expanded antigen-specific CD8 and CD4 T cells in vitro and in mice (Kreiter and colleagues). In a first-in-human RNA poly-neo-epitope melanoma study all patients developed T-cell responses against multiple vaccine neo-epitopes (Sahin and colleagues; abstract only), and each patient's vaccine in the Rojas pancreatic cancer trial used two uridine mRNA strands, each encoding up to 10 neoepitopes. Mass spectrometry can identify recovered HLA-bound peptides. Caron and colleagues' 2015 review describes class I peptides predominantly 9 to 12 amino acids long and reports that about 10 per cent of acquired spectra could be confidently assigned at a 1 per cent false discovery rate in the workflows discussed. It also describes evidence that mass spectrometry underestimates the self-HLA peptide repertoire, so non-detection does not prove absence. Prediction is not presentation: of more than 1,300 amino acid changes in two mouse tumour models about 13 per cent were predicted to bind MHC class I and a small fraction of those were confirmed by mass spectrometry (Yadav and colleagues). Because a single amino acid after an epitope changed its immunogenicity in a multiepitope DNA vaccine (Livingston and colleagues, already linked), a changed spacer is a changed construct that needs renewed processing and display evidence, while earlier evidence is retained for the parts that did not change.

remaining: Explicit A-only prior display and its inability to establish B or the revised construct.

proposedEvidenceNotCredited.supportingExcerpt: A spacer is an encoded amino-acid sequence between antigen windows, rather than an untranslated gap. A possible boundary peptide can contain part of a window and part of its spacer; encoding it does not establish that processing produces it, that HLA displays it or that a receptor recognises it. In an invented A-spacer-B comparison, replacing the spacer changes the combined protein. Earlier evidence of A display belongs to the earlier revision; it establishes neither B display nor the revised construct's display or tumour recognition.

proofs.requirement: Sequence order, nucleoside chemistry and unwanted byproducts are independent design/quality axes; the category diagram specifies no chemical structure or recipe.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A nucleoside combines a base with a sugar; a nucleotide also carries phosphate. Modified RNA building blocks change chemistry separately from the intended sequence and from contaminating byproducts. Characterise chemistry and identity, impurities, protein identity and quantity, and innate-sensing readouts under matched sequence, amount, cap, UTR, purity and formulation conditions. A translation or cytokine result cannot establish every later immune or clinical outcome.

proofs.requirement: An unchanged intended coding message does not establish the identity or fidelity of measured translation products.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In cell lines and mice, N1-methylpseudouridine, alone or with 5-methylcytidine, gave higher reporter expression than pseudouridine-based mRNA, up to about 44-fold for double-modified mRNA and about 13-fold for single-modified mRNA as the abstract reports (cell lines and mice respectively), with less innate immunogenicity and better cell viability in vitro (Andries and colleagues). Separately, N1-methylpseudouridine caused +1 ribosomal frameshifting in vitro at slippery sequences, cellular immunity to +1 products was found in mice and humans after vaccination with BNT162b2 vaccine mRNA, and synonymous changes at those sequences reduced frameshifted products; the authors note that no adverse outcomes from mistranslation of the SARS-CoV-2 vaccines have been reported (Mulroney and colleagues). More reporter signal with less cytokine in one matched comparison does not show a stronger antigen-specific T-cell response: unmodified mRNAs were translated better after purification yet still induced high cytokine secretion, and purified modified mRNA was translated 10 to 1000-fold more in primary cells (Karikó and colleagues, 2011), so sensing, expression and T-cell readouts each need their own evidence.

proofs.requirement: Chemistry can affect measured sensing and translation in defined systems without guaranteeing no sensing, more useful immunity or a universal improvement.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Chemical changes to RNA building blocks can alter how a message is sensed and translated. The effect depends on the RNA and the system in which it is tested.

Karikó's 2005 experiments compared human TLR systems and dendritic-cell readouts under selected nucleoside modifications. In the 2011 study, modified transcripts still contained activating contaminants including double-stranded RNA, and purification changed innate activation and translation. A change in building-block chemistry is therefore separate from removal of byproducts.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Primary experiments found that selected nucleoside modifications changed RNA-triggered innate immune activation. Later work showed that purification of modified transcripts also affected inflammatory responses and protein expression. Modification and removal of contaminants are therefore distinct design and manufacturing questions. Results from those experimental systems do not establish that one modification is best for every cancer vaccine, delivery platform or intended immune response.
